eagle.alt: A footpad and surface-sensing probe beneath Eagle on the Moon.
eagle.caption: NASA · AS11-40-5917, July 20, 1969: a close view of Eagle’s landing foot and surface-sensing probe during Apollo 11. This hardware belonged to the descent stage that stayed behind.

eagle.alt: Eagle’s separate ascent stage above the lunar surface, viewed from the command module.
eagle.caption: NASA · AS11-44-6626, July 21, 1969: Eagle’s ascent stage approaches the command and service modules in lunar orbit. The image shows the upper stage after it left the descent stage on the Moon.

surveyor3.alt: Surveyor 3’s footpad and sampler scoop photographed during Apollo 12.
surveyor3.caption: NASA · AS12-48-7110, November 20, 1969: Apollo 12 photographed Surveyor 3’s footpad, scoop and landing marks. Selected components were later carried to Earth; the complete lander was not returned.

surveyor3.alt: Returned Surveyor 3 components displayed in a NASA laboratory on Earth.
surveyor3.caption: NASA/Jim Grossmann · November 8, 2011: pieces retrieved from Surveyor 3 by Apollo 12 are examined at Kennedy Space Center’s Granular Mechanics and Regolith Operations Lab. This is Earth-based study of returned hardware.

alsep12.alt: Alan Bean deploying Apollo 12’s lunar experiment station.
alsep12.caption: NASA/Charles Conrad Jr. · AS12-47-6919, November 19, 1969: Alan Bean deploys components of Apollo 12’s ALSEP station. The photograph records the astronaut work needed before the instruments could operate after departure.

alsep12.alt: Alan Bean using a transfer tool beside the Apollo 12 Lunar Module.
alsep12.caption: NASA/Charles Conrad Jr. · AS12-46-6790, November 19, 1969: Alan Bean removes the fuel element for ALSEP’s radioisotope thermoelectric generator. The RTG provided electricity for the experiment station.

lrv.alt: An Apollo 17 rover close-up showing a repaired rear fender.
lrv.caption: NASA/Eugene Cernan · AS17-137-20979, December 12, 1972: a close-up of Apollo 17’s rover shows the improvised rear-fender repair using lunar maps and clamps. Harrison Schmitt sits in the vehicle.

lrv.alt: Earth visible above the Apollo 17 rover’s high-gain antenna.
lrv.caption: NASA/Harrison Schmitt · AS17-134-20473, December 13, 1972: Earth appears above the rover’s high-gain antenna at Taurus-Littrow. Eugene Cernan stands beside the vehicle during the crew’s third surface excursion.

reflector.alt: Buzz Aldrin carrying the reflector and seismic experiment across the lunar surface.
reflector.caption: NASA/Neil Armstrong · AS11-40-5942, July 20, 1969: Buzz Aldrin carries the laser reflector in his right hand and the passive seismic package in his left. The two instruments had different scientific jobs.

reflector.alt: The Apollo 11 laser reflector and seismic package deployed beyond astronaut footprints.
reflector.caption: NASA · AS11-37-5551, July 20, 1969: the deployed laser reflector is nearer the camera on the right, with the seismic package farther away. The view was taken from inside Eagle.

falcon.alt: Falcon just before its ascent stage lifted off, seen by the rover’s television camera.
falcon.caption: NASA · S71-41511, August 2, 1971: a frame from the rover-mounted television camera seconds before Falcon’s ascent-stage liftoff. Both stages are visible here; the lower descent stage remained after departure.

falcon.alt: The Hadley-Apennine landscape seen from Falcon’s upper hatch.
falcon.caption: NASA/David Scott · AS15-87-11748, July 31, 1971: a view toward Hadley Delta from Falcon’s upper hatch during the stand-up surface inspection. It provides mission-era landscape context for the landing site.

surveyor1.alt: A mosaic of Surveyor 1’s pictures of its lunar landing site.
surveyor1.caption: NASA/JPL · Surveyor 1, 1966: a mosaic of surface pictures from the Flamsteed P landing region in Oceanus Procellarum. It records the working mission’s surroundings, rather than a modern view.

source.title: Surveyor 1 surface and orbital image history

surveyor1.alt: A 2009 orbital image identifying Surveyor 1 and its shadow.
surveyor1.caption: NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University · LRO, 2009: Surveyor 1 and its shadow photographed from lunar orbit. This dated observation connects the mission’s surface images with the hardware’s later appearance.

source.title: Surveyor 1 surface and orbital image history

surveyor5.alt: Surveyor 5’s footpad and the trench made during its sloping landing.
surveyor5.caption: NASA/JPL · PIA02978, Surveyor 5 mission, 1967: a footpad rests beside a trench formed as it slid during landing in Mare Tranquillitatis. This is a mission-era close-up of the surface.

surveyor5.alt: A lunar map marking the five successful Surveyor landing sites.
surveyor5.caption: NASA · Historical Surveyor landing-site map reproduced in a January 2018 mission history. Surveyor 5 is one of five successful landings shown; this is geographical context, not a surface photograph.

surveyor6.alt: The Atlas-Centaur launch carrying Surveyor 6 into the night sky.
surveyor6.caption: NASA · Surveyor 6 launch, November 7, 1967: the spacecraft leaves Earth on its journey to Sinus Medii. This launch photograph precedes its lunar landing and short surface hop.

surveyor6.alt: A labelled Surveyor spacecraft diagram used as family-design context.
surveyor6.caption: NASA · Labelled Surveyor 1 engineering diagram, reproduced as Surveyor-family design context. It illustrates the general camera, support and landing arrangement; Surveyor 6’s instrument payload was different. This is not a photograph of retired hardware.

surveyor7.alt: Surveyor 7’s mosaic of lunar highlands near Tycho crater.
surveyor7.caption: NASA/JPL · Surveyor 7 mission, 1968: a mosaic of surface pictures near Tycho crater. The highland setting differed from earlier mare sites and supplied a new landscape for scientific comparison.

source.title: Surveyor 7 surface and orbital image history

surveyor7.alt: A later orbital view marking Surveyor 7’s landing site near Tycho.
surveyor7.caption: NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University · Later LROC view of the Surveyor 7 site near Tycho, reproduced in NASA’s January 2018 history. The marked site is a dated orbital observation, not a live view.

source.title: Surveyor 7 surface and orbital image history

opportunity.alt: Opportunity at Victoria crater from orbit
opportunity.caption: NASA/JPL/University of Arizona · PIA08812 — HiRISE orbital image of Opportunity beside Victoria crater, 2006. This historical view locates the rover at an earlier stop, not at its final resting place.

source.title: The Opportunity Rover at Victoria Crater

opportunity.alt: Opportunity wheel tracks inside Perseverance Valley
opportunity.caption: NASA/JPL-Caltech/Cornell Univ./Arizona State Univ. · PIA22074 — Opportunity’s Pancam mosaic, September 4–October 6, 2017, shows wheel tracks within Perseverance Valley. This is a historical mission view.

source.title: View From Within 'Perseverance Valley' on Mars

spirit.alt: Layered rocks in Spirit’s false-color Gibson panorama
spirit.caption: NASA/JPL-Caltech/USGS/Cornell University · PIA02689 — Spirit’s Gibson panorama at Home Plate, acquired February 9–12, 2006. False color emphasizes differences between rocks and soil; the curved mosaic is not a literal curved horizon.

source.title: Gibson Panorama by Spirit at Home Plate False Color

spirit.alt: Bright silica-rich soil uncovered along Spirit’s route
spirit.caption: NASA/JPL/Cornell · PIA09491 — Silica-rich soil investigated by Spirit in 2007, NASA archive release May 21, 2007. Mineral evidence helped researchers examine an ancient watery environment; it is not proof of life.

insight.alt: InSight’s wind and thermal shield covering its surface seismometer
insight.caption: NASA/JPL-Caltech · PIA22959 — InSight placed its wind and thermal shield over the seismometer on February 2, 2019. The instrument had been set on the ground in December 2018.

source.title: InSight Deploys its Wind and Thermal Shield

insight.caption: NASA/JPL-Caltech · PIA25287 — InSight’s final selfie, April 24, 2022, shows dust accumulated on the lander and its solar panels. Compare this historical image with the earlier, cleaner mission portrait.

viking1.alt: Low evening sunlight across the Viking 1 landing site
viking1.caption: NASA/JPL · PIA00567 — Viking 1’s view of Chryse Planitia about fifteen minutes before sunset on August 21, 1976. Low-angle sunlight reveals terrain that looks different at midday.

source.title: Sunset at the Viking Lander 1 Site

viking1.alt: Meteorology instrument on Viking 1 above the Martian ground
viking1.caption: NASA/JPL · PIA00392 — Viking 1’s meteorology instrument in a historical mission photograph. NASA archive entry PIA00392 was released December 12, 1996; that archive date is not a new surface observation.

source.title: The Meteorology Instrument on Viking Lander 1

phoenix.alt: Martian soil collected inside Phoenix’s robotic scoop
phoenix.caption: NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona/Max Planck Institute · PIA10745 — Phoenix’s robotic-arm camera shows soil inside the scoop after its first test dig, June 1, 2008 (sol 7). This close-up connects the arm model with a real sampling tool.

source.title: Martian Soil Inside Phoenix Robotic Arm Scoop

phoenix.alt: Phoenix’s solar array beside the robotic arm carrying a sample
phoenix.caption: NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona/Texas A&M University · PIA10793 — Phoenix’s solar panel and robotic arm with a sample in its scoop, June 2008. The photograph was made before delivery to the optical microscope.

source.title: Panorama of Phoenix Solar Panel and Robotic Arm

viking2.alt: Sunrise above the horizon at Viking 2’s Utopia Planitia site
viking2.caption: NASA/JPL/LaRC · PIA00576 — Viking 2 recorded this sunrise on June 14, 1978, sol 631. Bright bands and color separation come partly from the camera’s limited brightness levels; this is a historical observation, not a live view.

viking2.alt: Viking 2’s sampler working between rocks in a sequence of images
viking2.caption: NASA/JPL · PIA00145 — A Viking 2 surface-sampler sequence at the area nicknamed Bonneville Salt Flats. NASA’s archival release is dated December 15, 1996; these are historical mission images of sampling between rocks.

pathfinder.alt: Pathfinder’s stationary lander seen by the Sojourner rover
pathfinder.caption: NASA/JPL · PIA01121 — Sojourner’s rover camera looks back at the Pathfinder lander during the 1997 mission. The lander and rover are separate pieces of hardware left on Mars.

source.title: Sojourner Rover View of Pathfinder Lander

pathfinder.alt: Deflated Pathfinder airbags lying beside rocks and soil
pathfinder.caption: NASA/JPL · PIA00651 — Pathfinder’s deflated landing airbags and nearby terrain, 1997. The airbags cushioned arrival, then collapsed so the lander could open its petals.

sojourner.alt: Sojourner’s rear instrument touching the rock Yogi
sojourner.caption: NASA/JPL · PIA00766 — Sojourner places its alpha proton X-ray spectrometer against Yogi, shown in an Imager for Mars Pathfinder sequence from sols 8–10, July 1997.

sojourner.alt: Yogi and disturbed soil viewed from Sojourner’s own low camera
sojourner.caption: NASA/JPL · PIA00998 — A rover-height view from Sojourner on sol 70, 1997. Wheel cleats and disturbed soil appear in the foreground, with Yogi farther away; this differs from the lander’s high viewpoint.

ingenuity.alt: Shadow of Ingenuity’s damaged rotor blade after its final flight
ingenuity.caption: NASA/JPL-Caltech · PIA26243 — Ingenuity photographed the shadow of a damaged rotor blade after flight 72 on January 18, 2024. This dated observation helped establish why the helicopter could no longer fly.

source.title: Ingenuity Spots the Shadow of Its Damaged Rotor Blade

ingenuity.alt: Ingenuity at its final airfield photographed from Perseverance
ingenuity.caption: NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU/MSSS · PIA26236 — Perseverance’s Mastcam-Z mosaic locates Ingenuity at its final airfield on February 4, 2024. This enhanced-color image emphasizes subtle color differences and is not a live view.

source.title: Perseverance Spots Ingenuity at Its Final Airfield

polarlander.alt: Global visualization of the proposed Mars Polar Lander target region
polarlander.caption: NASA/JPL · PIA02315 — Proposed Mars Polar Lander landing region in a global-perspective visualization, released August 26, 1999. This is pre-arrival planning context; the lander’s actual resting place remains unconfirmed.

source.title: Proposed Mars Polar Lander Landing Site Global Perspective

polarlander.alt: Perspective visualization of the intended Mars Polar Lander region
polarlander.caption: NASA/JPL · PIA02316 — Perspective visualization of the proposed landing region, released August 26, 1999. It illustrates the intended destination, not a verified landing site or a photograph of recovered hardware.

source.title: Proposed Mars Polar Lander Landing Site Perspective View 1

intro.label: NASA / LRO · Lunar flyover visualization
intro.caption: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter–based NASA visualization, released in 2018. ECHOES made this silent forward-and-reverse loop from the title-free animation; it is not live footage.
intro.alt: A NASA data-based camera view approaches the Moon’s cratered terrain and sunlit horizon.

source.title: Tour of the Moon 4K Redux
source.org: NASA Goddard Scientific Visualization Studio / Ernie Wright; LRO data

intro.editing: Ten seconds played forward, then in reverse to make a continuous twenty-second decorative loop. Original soundtrack is absent; no licensed music is included.

clips.title: A helicopter flies on another planet
clips.alt: Ingenuity hovering above rocky Martian ground, filmed by the Perseverance rover.
clips.caption: Historical footage of Ingenuity’s first flight, April 19, 2021. Silent excerpt cropped for visibility; the playback speed is unchanged. This is a working-mission record, not a current view.

source.title: First Video of NASA’s Ingenuity Mars Helicopter in Flight

clips.editing: Cropped to central 640×360 region and resized to 960×540; audio removed, playback speed unchanged.

clips.title: A hammer, a feather, and a lunar lesson
clips.alt: Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott demonstrates a hammer-and-feather drop on the lunar surface.
clips.caption: Apollo 15 mission context: David Scott’s hammer-and-feather demonstration on the Moon, August 2, 1971. Silent NASA television excerpt. This demonstrates surface science during Falcon’s mission; it is not a video of the descent stage’s current condition.

source.title: The Apollo 15 Hammer-Feather Drop
source.org: NASA / National Space Science Data Center

clips.editing: 35-second excerpt, resized to 640×480; audio removed, playback speed unchanged.

clips.title: An arm places science on the ground
clips.alt: A NASA animation shows InSight’s articulated arm moving an instrument toward the surface of Mars.
clips.caption: NASA pre-mission visualization of InSight’s planned instrument deployment, published in 2017. This illustrates the design and intended tasks, rather than recorded deployment footage.

source.title: Animation of the InSight Spacecraft Lander

clips.editing: 30-second excerpt, resized to 854×480; audio removed, playback speed unchanged.

clips.title: Six wheels leave their first ramp
clips.alt: A sequence of Pathfinder lander images shows Sojourner rolling down its deployment ramp onto Mars.
clips.caption: Pathfinder lander images show Sojourner’s rollout in July 1997. The short image sequence is repeated three times for viewing; it is not real-time video. NASA/IMP Team/JPL.

source.title: Sojourner On Mars — NASA Astronomy Picture of the Day, July 7, 1997

clips.editing: NASA GIF image sequence repeated three times and encoded as silent MP4. No motion interpolation; images are held at their source timing. Original 256×248 images were resized to 512×496; no extra image detail was generated.

optionalIntroPhoto.label: Apollo 8 Earthrise
optionalIntroPhoto.caption: Earthrise photographed from Apollo 8, December 24, 1968. NASA/William Anders, AS08-14-2383. Optional separate still, not the source of the LRO video.
optionalIntroPhoto.alt: Blue-and-white Earth above the grey lunar horizon against black space.

source.title: Apollo 8 Mission image, Earth over the horizon of the moon

video.runtime: All MP4s are silent H.264/yuv420p with fast-start metadata. Story videos require user playback. Intro may be muted/decorative only; use its matching poster for reduced motion. VTT tracks are original visual descriptions, not transcribed speech.

note: NASA-derived historical records and labelled visualizations, not live views. Video soundtracks removed; films play only after a visitor selects them. Intro silent loop respects motion/data preferences.
